pages.title: OBT Consultant Development Track
pages.metaDescription: The OBT Consultant Development Track raises up certified consultants for oral Bible translation through genre-based workshops, mentorship, and competency-based certification.

blocks.title: Consultants for a Bible that is spoken, not read
blocks.body:
Oral Bible translation is growing faster than any form of Bible translation ever has. The consultants who safeguard its quality are still far too few.

The OBT Consultant Development Track forms and certifies consultants for this work: in community, through real practice, at the pace of genuine readiness.

blocks.title: Certification based on readiness, not seat time
blocks.body:
This track certifies oral Bible translation consultants when they demonstrate the full set of consulting competencies, wherever and however they gained them.

We call it the roundabout model. Instead of a fixed sequence of required courses, the track is a circulation: people enter from different directions, keep moving while they grow, and exit when a mentor confirms they are ready.

blocks.title: Training is usually drawn as a straight road
blocks.body:
Attend the courses in order, pass the milestones, arrive at certification. A straight road works well when everyone starts from the same place and can travel on the same schedule.

OBT consultants do not start from the same place. They come from many nations and ministries, carry very different training histories, and most are already serving translation projects they cannot simply leave for a year of coursework.

blocks.title: So we built a roundabout
blocks.body:
A roundabout has many entry roads. A field translator with years of experience, an exegete from a partner organization, a consultant adding an oral specialization: each enters from where they actually are, usually through our experiential OBT Crash Course or equivalent experience.

No one is sent back to the start of someone else's road. And no one has to stop serving their projects in order to keep moving.

blocks.title: Five threads at once
blocks.body:
Circulating means growing along five threads at once: genre-based workshops that act as catalysts, online trainings between them, biblical language cohorts, ongoing mentorship, and supervised practice on real translation projects.

Every lap adds evidence. A workshop evaluation here, a mentored consultant check there, a language milestone, a teaching assignment. The track keeps that evidence, competency by competency.

blocks.title: Progress you can actually see
blocks.body:
Every workshop activity is tied to specific, observable competencies. Multiple facilitators record what they see each participant do, then translate those observations into simple 0 to 3 ratings against SIL's Competency-Based Consulting matrix.

Because many evaluators watch many activities over weeks of intense collaboration, the picture is rich and hard to fake, and it is verified by the facilitators before anything enters a participant's record.

blocks.title: The exit is readiness, confirmed by a mentor
blocks.body:
Workshop scores never certify anyone. Each participant has a consultant-mentor who walks with them, weighs all the evidence, and confirms when the full competency set is genuinely in place. That confirmation is the exit ramp.

Some people exit after a few laps; others circulate longer. On a roundabout, that is not falling behind. It is how the model is supposed to work.

blocks.title: Graduates come back as mentors
blocks.body:
The first cycle aims to certify 25 OBT-specialized consultants. But graduates do not simply drive away: strong participants return as session leaders, mentors, and workshop facilitators for the next generation.

The goal is not one cohort of consultants. It is a sustainable, replicable pathway that regions can carry forward themselves.

blocks.title: See how the track works
blocks.body: The pages below take each part of the model in turn: why the track exists, how certification works, and what the five threads look like in practice.

pages.title: Why this track exists
pages.metaDescription: Oral Bible translation has grown explosively, and the consultants who safeguard its quality are scarce. Why the OBT Consultant Development Track was built, and the principles that shape it.

blocks.title: Why this track exists
blocks.body: Oral Bible translation went from about 20 active projects to more than 1,200 in six years. The consultants who check that work did not multiply with it.

blocks.title: The fastest growth Bible translation has ever seen
blocks.body:
In roughly 120 years, written Bible translation grew from about 10 active projects to about 800. Oral Bible translation grew from about 20 active projects to more than 1,200 in six years.

The reason is impact. In an OBT project, a team of mature believers internalizes long sections of Scripture and translates them from memory, orally, into the heart language of their community. By the time a book is finished, the community has orally processed every passage many times over.

items.body: These translators end up holding entire books of the Bible in memory. In their communities, they are often called walking Bibles.
items.attribution: Why OBT projects multiply so quickly

blocks.title: Growth has outrun quality assurance
blocks.body:
Every Bible translation project needs consultants: experienced practitioners who check the translation with the team so that what the community receives is accurate, clear, and natural. OBT projects have multiplied faster than the consulting pool can sustain, and the pool of consultants equipped to evaluate specifically oral translation meets only a small fraction of the need.

There is a deeper problem than headcount. Nearly all existing consultant training was built around literacy: written commentaries, written drafts, written feedback. Oral Bible translation follows an oral method and produces an oral product, so its consultants need a substantially different repertoire of analytical, relational, and intuitive skills.

items.title: Performance carries meaning
items.body: Intonation, pacing, and emotional expression all bear on whether a translation communicates faithfully. Consultants must evaluate dimensions of meaning that never appear in a written back translation.

items.title: Each genre raises different problems
items.body: Checking a narrative means attending to story flow and participant reference; checking a psalm means understanding Hebrew poetics and local artistic genres. The skills differ so much by genre that the whole workshop series is organized around genres.

items.title: Contexts vary enormously
items.body: Some consultants work face to face with community performers; others work virtually with teams in restricted-access areas. Different workflows and checking technologies place very different demands on the consultant.

items.title: Consultants serve many languages
items.body: Most OBT consultants serve multiple language communities without deep knowledge of any single one, so training focuses on transferable analytical frameworks and consulting postures rather than language-specific knowledge.

blocks.title: Three principles behind the curriculum
blocks.body: Everything in the track flows from a single commitment: start with orality, and design everything else around it. Three working principles carry that commitment into each workshop.

items.title: Teach what cannot be gained elsewhere
items.body: Excellent resources already cover biblical languages, linguistics, and Bible background, and we point participants to them. Precious in-person time goes to what those resources do not provide: OBT-specific exegesis, oral genre discovery, checking practice, and the formation of a consulting identity.

items.title: Practice first, theory layered on
items.body: Participants exegete, internalize, draft, revise, and prepare for checking inside every workshop, with corrective feedback at each step. Having wrestled with a genre from the inside, they can later speak into its challenges with earned authority.

items.title: Model the methods consultants will use
items.body: The workshops deliberately teach through oral, experiential, discussion-based methods that participants can turn around and use with their own translation teams, rather than defaulting to lecture.

pages.title: How certification works
pages.metaDescription: The OBT-CDT certifies consultants through the Competency-Based Consulting method: observable evidence, a 0 to 3 rubric, multiple evaluators, and a mentor who confirms readiness.

blocks.title: How certification works
blocks.body: Certification here rests on what evaluators actually watched a participant do, scored against SIL's competency matrix and confirmed by a mentor who knows their work.

blocks.title: Competency-based consulting in plain terms
blocks.body:
SIL maintains a matrix of the competencies a Bible translation consultant needs: exegesis, discourse analysis, consulting process skills, interpersonal skills, technology, and more. Competency-Based Consulting (CBC) is the discipline of certifying people against that matrix using documented evidence, rather than against a list of courses attended.

The track is built on the method itself. The particular platform that stores the records may evolve, but the discipline stays the same: name the competency, observe real behavior, document the evidence, and let a mentor weigh it.

blocks.title: How observations become evidence
blocks.body:
Before each workshop, every lesson and activity is tied to specific knowledge, skills, and attitudes (KSAs), each connected to observable phenomena, so evaluators know exactly what to watch and listen for.

During the workshop, facilitators record descriptive notes on what they actually see each participant do. Observations from multiple facilitators across many activities come together in one structured record per participant, which makes the resulting picture far richer than any single observer could produce.

items.title: Observations become simple 0 to 3 ratings
items.body: Qualitative observation comes first; the numbers summarize it. Each rating is tied to a specific competency sub-point and is reviewed by facilitators who verify that it reflects what they saw.

items.label: Not yet observed
items.body: No evidence for this competency yet. A starting point, not a judgment.

items.label: Emerging
items.body: Early evidence is present; the participant needs substantial support in this area.

items.label: Developing
items.body: Solid, repeated evidence; the participant works well with light support.

items.label: Established
items.body: Consistent, independent competence, confirmed across activities and evaluators.
A workshop is both a fishbowl and a pressure cooker. Across weeks of intense multicultural teamwork, real strengths and real growth areas both come clearly into view.

items.title: Continuous observation
items.body: Facilitators watch and note evidence throughout activities, tagged to the participant or group it belongs to.

items.title: Processing the day
items.body: The facilitation team reviews and consolidates the day's observations while they are fresh.

items.title: A written evaluation
items.body: Each participant receives a written evaluation, drafted from the shared record and verified by multiple facilitators.

items.title: Evidence enters the record
items.body: Verified evidence is submitted into the participant's competency record, organized so their mentor can see what was observed, at what level, and by whom.

blocks.title: The mentor decides
blocks.body:
Workshop scores are evidence, never a verdict. Each participant's consultant-mentor talks the evidence through with them, weighs it alongside field experience, and assigns the final ratings at their own discretion. Certification happens when the mentor confirms the full competency set is in place.

This is what makes the roundabout model trustworthy: the track generates unusually rich, verified evidence, and a human being who knows the participant makes the call.

pages.title: The Five Threads
pages.metaDescription: Five interlocking threads form OBT consultants: genre-based workshops, online trainings, biblical language cohorts, ongoing mentorship, and field-based application.

blocks.title: The Five Threads
blocks.body: Workshops are the visible part, and on their own they would not be enough. Formation runs along five threads at once, and every one of them produces evidence.

blocks.title: Formation happens in five ways at once
blocks.body:
Competency development in the track is distributed across five interlocking threads. Together they provide training and mentorship sufficient to meet the full set of consulting competencies.

Participants are not expected to engage every thread in equal measure. Each person draws most heavily on the threads that will most effectively advance their own readiness, which is exactly what the roundabout model is for.

items.title: Workshops
items.body: Five two-week intensives, each centered on a major biblical genre: Narrative, Epistles, Psalms, Legal Texts in the Torah, and Prophecy and Wisdom Literature. Participants practice most consulting competencies inside the genre at hand, with feedback at every step.

items.title: Online training
items.body: Between workshops, live virtual sessions target the competencies the previous workshop showed participants most need, alongside curated self-paced material. Wherever possible these run with cohort elements, so no one studies alone.

items.title: Biblical language cohorts
items.body: Participants build Hebrew and Greek competence through structured coursework with guidance from a biblical-language mentor, cohort-style. The workshops apply that knowledge to oral translation; the cohorts build the foundation.

items.title: Ongoing mentorship
items.body: Each consultant-in-training works with an assigned consultant-mentor who monitors development, guides growth, and ultimately validates readiness for certification, supported by feedback from many consultants and subject-matter experts along the way.

items.title: Field practice
items.body: Participants observe practicing OBT consultants and conduct supervised consultant checks on real translation projects. Strong participants are also trained to lead crash-course sessions for the next round, deepening mastery by teaching.

blocks.title: Most of the formation happens between workshops
blocks.body:
Workshops act as catalysts: two weeks that ignite skills and expose exactly where each participant should grow next. But the track depends equally on what happens between them: the virtual sessions, the language cohorts, the mentor conversations, and the supervised checks on real projects.

Evaluation data from each workshop feeds directly into what gets taught between workshops, so the track adapts to the actual cohort rather than to a fixed syllabus.

pages.title: The workshop series
pages.metaDescription: Five two-week, genre-based workshops anchor the OBT Consultant Development Track: Narrative, Epistles, Psalms, Legal Texts in the Torah, and Prophecy and Wisdom Literature.

blocks.title: The workshop series
blocks.body: Five two-week workshops anchor the track, one for each genre. Each is a fortnight of real translation work with consultants watching.

blocks.title: Every workshop runs the same way
blocks.body:
Each workshop moves through genre-specific instruction, hands-on translation experience, and supervised consulting practice. Participants exegete, internalize, draft, revise, and check within the two weeks, so competencies are practiced rather than merely presented.

The series progresses from more accessible genres toward more complex ones, and the one-week experiential OBT Crash Course is the recommended doorway for newcomers: each crash-course participant learns oral Bible translation by doing it, functioning as a mother-tongue translator for a week.

items.title: 1 · Narrative · Bangalore, India
items.body: Foundational OBT translation skills, OBT-specific exegesis, internalization, and introductory consulting awareness.

items.title: 2 · Epistles · Chiang Mai, Thailand
items.body: Argument structure and prominence in the Epistles, with structured consulting practice on a real OBT translation.

items.title: 3 · Psalms · Bali, Indonesia
items.body: Hebrew poetry exegesis for OBT and the facilitation of Psalms translation into local artistic genres.

items.title: 4 · Legal Texts in the Torah
items.body: Legal and sacrificial codes in the Torah and the genre-specific consulting challenges they present.

items.title: 5 · Prophecy and Wisdom Literature
items.body: Prophetic and wisdom literature, and consolidation of the full consulting skill set. Prophecy follows the legal texts because it so often depends on the Torah's covenantal material.

blocks.title: You can join for a single workshop
blocks.body: Visiting one workshop is an effective way to assess whether the track fits a mentee, to add an oral specialization to an existing consulting certification, or to contribute as a session leader or evaluator.

pages.title: Help form the next OBT consultants
pages.metaDescription: The OBT Consultant Development Track needs OBT consultant-mentors, mentors in linguistics and biblical languages, checking opportunities on real projects, and sponsorship partners.

blocks.title: Help form the next OBT consultants
blocks.body: Participants are already serving translation projects across more than eight nations. What most of them lack is someone experienced enough to check their work and walk with them.

blocks.title: A track like this runs on people who give their skill away
blocks.body:
Our participants are capable, motivated, and already serving oral Bible translation projects across more than eight nations. What stands between many of them and certification is not ability. It is access: to mentors, to supervised practice, and to the kind of sustained relationships that form consultants.

If you carry experience in Bible translation consulting, linguistics, or the biblical languages, there is a concrete place for you here.

items.title: Mentor as an OBT consultant
items.body: Our most pressing need. Practicing OBT consultants who will take on one or more consultants-in-training: monitoring their development, guiding their growth, and ultimately confirming their readiness for certification.

items.title: Mentor in linguistics or biblical languages
items.body: Participants build linguistics and Hebrew or Greek competence through guided self-study and cohorts. Mentors in these disciplines answer questions, review progress, and keep cohorts moving with encouragement and accountability.

items.title: Open a checking opportunity
items.body: If you lead or advise an OBT project, hosting a supervised consultant check gives a consultant-in-training the real practice they cannot get any other way, under the eye of an experienced consultant, at no cost to your project's quality.

items.title: Sponsor and partner
items.body: Most participants serve with organizations of limited means, and the track actively seeks partners to keep workshops affordable for them. Sponsorship conversations, large or small, are warmly welcome.

blocks.title: Who you would be serving
blocks.body: The current cohort is drawn from over eight nations, and most participants serve with Asian organizations of limited means. They are field translators, exegetes, and translation advisors who bring years of real project experience and are pressing toward the consulting competencies their movements urgently need.

blocks.title: Get in touch
blocks.body: Write a few lines about who you are and how you hope to contribute, and we will follow up personally.

pages.title: The OBT Crash Course
pages.metaDescription: Participant handbook for the OBT Crash Course, Bali, 18 to 22 August 2026: why the course is built the way it is, what happens each day, and what each session is for.

blocks.title: The OBT Crash Course
blocks.body: Five days that give a cohort one shared account of what oral Bible translation is and how it is actually done. This page is the handbook for it: why the course is built the way it is, what each day holds, and what every session is for.
blocks.note: Last updated 18 August 2026 · the daily timetable is now on this page, in section three. Where an older email disagrees with this page, the page is right.

items.label: University of the Nations base, Jimbaran, Bali

blocks.title: Learn the whole process by running it twice
blocks.body:
Most training in Bible translation teaches a step at a time and hopes the steps add up. This course does the opposite. In five days you take a passage from first reading to a consultant-checked recording, and then, on the last day, you do the whole thing again on a second passage with the teaching taken away.

That is the design. Every teaching session is short and is followed immediately by the work it describes, because the skill this track certifies is not knowing what internalisation is. It is being able to lead it.

blocks.caption: A recordist at work in the field. Everything this week rehearses points at a room like this one.

items.label: What you will be able to do

blocks.title: Why this course exists
blocks.body:
Oral Bible translation is not written translation read aloud. It is a different process producing a different product for a different kind of audience, and a consultant who has only ever checked a printed text will reach for the wrong questions in the room.

The Crash Course exists to give everyone on this track the same starting account of that difference: what makes a process oral, what makes a product oral, and where the line is beyond which neither is true any more. Everything that follows in the series, including the Psalms workshop next week, assumes you have this week's vocabulary and this week's experience of having done the work yourself.

Five convictions shape how the days are built. They are worth reading before the week starts, because they explain why sessions are short, why you will spend more time working than listening, and why you will be asked to do the same thing twice.

items.label: Course thesis
items.title: Orality is not the absence of literacy. It is a preference for holistic communication, and it has been the primary way people think and communicate throughout history.
items.body: We treat it as a beautiful aspect of how God made human beings, how he has acted in sacred history, and how he has grown his church, rather than as a problem to work around. Almost every practical decision this week follows from taking that seriously.

items.title: The better a team understands the passage, the less goes wrong later
items.body:
This is the principle the week is built on, and it is the reason exegesis comes first and gets the most time. Mistakes that are cheap to fix in an exegesis conversation are expensive in a draft and painful in a recording, because an oral draft cannot be quietly edited. Somebody has to re-internalise it.

So the exegesis you do here is holistic rather than lexical: eight areas of inquiry, seven from the OBT article by Frost, Mustin and Beal, plus the cultural and historical background as the eighth.

items.title: The purpose of the translation shapes the process, not only the product
items.body:
A team's goal for its community decides what an adequate process looks like: how oral the community actually is, which steps have to change, and by how much. A consultant's job is to reason about that with the team rather than to apply a fixed sequence and score it.

You will be asked repeatedly this week to say why a step should change for a given community, not only that it should.

items.title: We teach the way we are asking you to teach
items.body:
The sessions model the adult-learning practices you will be expected to use with mother-tongue translators: conversation rather than lecture, simple repeatable symbols you can draw on a whiteboard, discovery before definition, and hooks back to the devotion earlier that morning.

If a session feels like it is being done to you rather than at you, that is the point. Watch the facilitation as well as the content, because you are the one who will be running it next.

items.title: The process is a chain of quality checks, and each link catches what no other link would
items.body: Exegesis, internalisation, drafting, recording, peer review, revision, community testing, the consultant check, and revision again. Every one of them exists to catch a particular kind of failure. A team under deadline pressure will always be tempted to cut one, and knowing what each step is for is what lets you say what that cut would cost.

items.title: Character is part of the competence
items.body:
Godly interaction inside the team, and between the team and the community, is the foundation the whole process rests on rather than a nice addition to it. Peer review, revision and the consultant check are the sessions where that becomes visible, because they are the sessions where somebody tells you your work is not finished.

We are asking each other for humility, unity, and a heart of service, and we will be paying attention to it.

items.title: What we are asking of each other this week

items.label: Do the work in your team rather than watching it. Facilitators are a resource, not a substitute.
Say when you are lost. A misunderstanding surfaced on Tuesday is cheap; the same one found on Saturday is not.
Give feedback somebody can act on. Point at a place in the recording and say what you heard there.
Receive feedback on the merits. Either change the draft, or say why the current rendering is right.
Keep the equipment and the files in order. Somebody else has to be able to find your work.

blocks.title: What you will be able to do
blocks.body: The course is organised around five areas of knowledge, attitude and skill. Each maps onto competencies in SIL's Competency-Based Consulting standard, which is the standard this whole track certifies against, so the work you do this week is evidence rather than practice for evidence.

items.value: Define it, and reason from it
items.body: Assess how oral a people group actually is, and think critically about a team's stated workflow in the light of it. Tell an oral Bible translation from an audio recording of a written one, in both process and product.

items.value: Name the steps and who holds them
items.body: State the core processes of an OBT workflow in order, say what each one is for, and describe the competencies and relationships a team needs at every step.
Do all three yourself on a real passage, to a standard a team could work from, and be able to facilitate them for others.
Give and receive hard feedback in a way that keeps the conversation open and separates the translation from the translator.
Use Audio Project Manager to carry an OBT process end to end, with Audacity alongside it, and reach the exegetical resources from FIA and the Spoken English Bible.

items.title: How the week is assessed
items.body:
Nine questions, spread across the five areas and asked at the sessions where the evidence actually appears. Facilitators record against them as the week goes, in the evaluation app, rather than writing a report afterwards from memory.

The scale has four points and matches the CBC scale. What separates the top two points is teaching capacity: whether you could model this for a mother-tongue team, not whether you did it tidily.

items.label: 0 · Not yet
items.value: What was produced would need to be redone rather than refined.

items.label: 1 · Emerging
items.value: The idea is visible but the execution is not. A facilitator can see what you were reaching for and would have to supply the rest.

items.label: 2 · Competent
items.value: You could do this on a real project with a colleague available for questions.

items.label: 3 · Strong
items.value: You could model it for a translation team, anticipating what will go wrong rather than only handling what does.

items.label: Where the bar sits
items.title: Two is the standard this course targets, not the middle of the range
items.body: A 2 means a competent consultant-in-training. Nobody is expected to arrive at a 3 across the board in five days, and a 1 in an area you have never worked in is information rather than a verdict.

items.title: What this week does not assess
items.body: Two things, said plainly so that nobody reads more into a Crash Course record than it holds. There is no session in which you teach this material to a translation team, so the week measures you doing the work rather than facilitating it; that evidence is collected in the Psalms workshop and later. And the exegesis question grades your written notes rather than your handling of an exegesis conversation, which is the largest thing this course still wants a home for.

blocks.title: The week at a glance
blocks.body:
Five full days, Tuesday to Saturday rather than Monday to Friday, because Monday the 17th is Indonesia's Independence Day. The course guide numbers the days One to Five, and so does this page.

Every day starts at 8:30, breaks mid-morning for a snack and at 1:00 for lunch, and closes at 4:00. Day One is the one exception at the start: the welcome comes first and the devotion follows it. Teaching sessions are short. The long blocks are yours, working in your team on the passage, with facilitators circulating. On the days when the work is not finished at 4:00, we take the snack and keep going.

All times are WITA, on the base.
blocks.caption: The long afternoon blocks are the course. The teaching sessions exist to set them up.

items.body: Internalisation for OBT, two hours internalising Passage 1, then Audio Project Manager and Audacity in the afternoon.

items.label: Draft, record, review, revise
items.body: The longest day of the workflow. Drafting, recording Passage 1 in APM, peer review, and a first revision.

items.label: Community testing and the consultant check
items.body: Building community testing questions in the morning, then a consultant check on your passage and a second revision across the rest of the day.

items.label: The whole process, again
items.body: A guided reflection on the process as a whole, then Passage 2 from exegesis to recording with the teaching taken away, and a celebration.

items.title: One thing to have done before Day Two
items.body: Every participant needs an Audio Project Manager account, APM downloaded, and verified entry into their team's translation project. If any of those three is not true for you, come to the Monday evening or the Tuesday lunch break and we will get it sorted before the Wednesday afternoon session, which assumes it.

blocks.title: Day One: orality and exegesis
blocks.body:
8:30 welcome and overview · 9:15 devotion · 9:45 orality and OBT · 11:00 snack · 11:30 exegesis for OBT · 1:00 lunch · 2:30 exegesis of Passage 1 · 4:00 close, notes in by the end of the evening.

Today builds the frame everything else hangs on, and then puts you straight to work inside it.

items.title: Welcome and overview
items.body: Viji welcomes the cohort, gives the history of the OBT Consultant Development Track and states what it is for. Josh leads introductions. The purpose is community and orientation: who is in the room, how this week connects to the last workshop and the next one, and where oral Bible translation sits inside the wider translation movement.

items.title: What is oral Bible translation, and what does it take?
items.body:
The definitional session, and the one the rest of the week refers back to. We build the definition of orality up from a few activities rather than starting from a slide, then take it into Bible translation: what would make a process an OBT process, when a process stops being one, what makes the product oral, and when it stops being that.

We compare what the group produces against a defined OBT process drawn with the symbols from the YWAM OBT handbook. Draw them. You will use them all week.

items.title: Exegesis for oral Bible translation
items.body:
The requirements for exegesis when the product will be heard rather than read. We start from Harmelink's account of multimodality and functionally cognitive semantics, told as a story, and work out the steps a facilitator needs to lead a holistic and conversational exegesis session.

If you come from a written translation background, this session is mostly about where the emphasis moves rather than what gets added. There is also a note here worth catching: on projects with no translation advisor, the OBT consultant often carries part of that role, and this is one of the places you build toward it.

items.title: Exegete Passage 1
items.body:
No new content. Your team applies the framework to the first passage, with facilitators available as a resource rather than as leaders. Notes are handed in by the end of the evening and read for technical accuracy and coverage of the eight areas, and you get them back in time to fix anything before internalisation.

Write them for the person who has to draft from them tomorrow, because that person is you.

blocks.title: Day Two: internalisation and the tools
blocks.body:
8:30 devotion · 9:00 internalisation for OBT · 10:30 snack · 11:00 internalise Passage 1 · 1:00 lunch and chores · 2:30 APM and Audacity training.

A teaching session, a long block of practice, and then the software that will carry the rest of the week.

items.title: Internalisation for OBT
items.body:
What internalisation is for, what tools it uses, and how to lead a session of it. Three things come together here: a cognitive-linguistics account of how meaning is made across several modes at once, which picks up Harmelink from yesterday; Katie Frost's 4Es framework for the process itself; and the SENSES acronym for organising the activities inside a session.

The session is run using the frameworks it is teaching, and it hooks back to the devotions, which is the clearest example this week of modelling the pedagogy we are asking for.

items.title: Internalise Passage 1
items.body:
Two hours in your team on the passage you exegeted yesterday. Facilitators watch and give feedback as you go, and this is a rated session: what is being looked for is deliberate use of the activities rather than reading the passage until it sticks, and whether you can tell the passage without the text while holding its structure, its participants and the flow of events.

Where something drops out, notice what dropped and go back for it. That noticing is most of the skill.

items.title: Audio Project Manager and Audacity
items.body:
A live walkthrough of APM on screen while you follow on your own machine, plus Audacity as the companion tool. We also cover why APM rather than Render or AVTT for this workshop, which comes down to its flexibility and to the team's experience with it, and we verify that everybody is properly set up in their own translation project.

What is assessed here is not speed. It is whether your files land in the right place for the right passage and your comments attach to the point they refer to, so that a peer reviewer can open your project on Thursday and work without asking you anything.

blocks.title: Day Three: draft, record, review, revise
blocks.body:
8:30 devotion with Viji · 9:00 drafting in OBT · 9:45 recording Passage 1 in APM · 11:00 snack · 11:30 peer review in APM · 1:00 lunch · 2:30 revise Passage 1 · 4:00 snack and work until it is done.

Four steps of the workflow in one day. The teaching is deliberately brief in each case so that the doing starts immediately.

items.title: Drafting in OBT
items.body:
Forty-five minutes on the role of drafting and its best practices, then straight into it. We return to the definition of OBT and place drafting inside the community's engagement with the meaning of the text, which by now has already happened in exegesis and internalisation.

The practical core is the sentence-draft file: a record of what the team thinks is best, roughly phrase by phrase, and then a whole-part-whole sequence of iterative performances whose best parts are stitched into a natural, faithful, clear and acceptable whole. We will also be honest about where the phrase-draft approach fits badly, because for some oral peoples it does.

items.title: Recording Passage 1 in APM
items.body:
Take the draft into APM and produce a recording. Getting a draft to a recordable state is itself the content of this session, because it is where the cost of a shaky internalisation becomes obvious: an oral passage cannot be quietly corrected later, since a change has to be re-memorised and re-performed before it can be recorded.

Assessment here is a completion check. Either the recording exists in the right place or it does not.

items.title: Peer review in APM
items.body:
The first quality check from outside your own team. A short orientation on what peer review is for within the broader checking community and what kinds of notes are actually useful, then you review another team's passage and they review yours.

A useful note points at a specific place in the recording and says what the reviewer heard there, in terms the other team can act on. General approval and general criticism are equally unusable.

items.title: Revise Passage 1
items.body:
The first test of whether a team can reason through translation issues under critique, which is why conduct is watched here as closely as craft. A short orientation on revision strategy comes first: give the community a version as close to final as you can, because a rough recording produces feedback that is not worth much; edit a phrase or two in so the new version can be played; then use that new audio as the basis for re-memorising.

Re-memorising the revised version is the step teams skip, and it is the one that produces the stronger recording for the community check.

blocks.title: Day Four: community testing and the consultant check
blocks.body:
8:30 devotion with Nikki · 9:00 making community testing questions · 10:30 snack · 11:00 consultant check and second revision, running through to 4:00 with a break for lunch · 4:00 snack and work until complete.

Today the passage leaves the team twice: once toward the community, at least on paper, and once toward a consultant.

items.title: Making community testing questions for OBT
items.body:
How community testing in OBT differs from community testing in written translation. Functionally the gap is smaller than people expect, especially for teams already used to reading a translation aloud. The real difference is that the audience is also asked about the emotion and the performance, because performance is part of an oral translation in a way it never is in a written one.

We reason toward that rather than announce it. Each team then writes five to ten questions and a general plan for how testing would be run, and hands both in.

items.title: Consultant check and second revision
items.body:
An OBT consultant gives consultant-level feedback on your passage, and you revise it. The check is lighter than a real one, on purpose. What matters is that you know what an OBT checking session feels like from both chairs: what a consultant asks and how they ask it, and what it is like to receive that and then go and change your translation.

The consultant is modelling the session you will practise running yourself in the Psalms workshop next week. Watch the facilitation, not only the notes.

items.title: If you finish early
items.body: Teams that get through the second revision with time left can begin exegesis on the next passage. Ask a facilitator before you start, so that we know where each team is going into Saturday.

blocks.title: Day Five: the whole process, again
blocks.body:
8:30 devotion and guided reflection with Josh · 9:00 the OBT process: steps, skills and relationships · 10:30 snack · the rest of the day on Passage 2, then celebration.

The last day has two halves. The first stands back and looks at the whole process at once. The second runs it again, faster, with no teaching in front of it.

items.title: The OBT process: steps, skills and relationships
items.body:
Ninety minutes of reflection conversation, and the only session all week that puts the entire process and its roles in front of the group at once. We name the steps in order, say what quality problem each one exists to catch, and work out what competencies and what relationships a real team needs at every step, including what a team does when nobody holds a needed competency.

It comes before the second passage rather than after it, deliberately. Reasoning about the whole process on the strength of four days of having worked it is a different thing from debriefing a fresh repetition.

items.title: Passage 2, start to finish
items.body:
Exegesis, internalisation, drafting and recording on a second passage, in one day, in your team. Facilitators will give light feedback if you ask for it, but the aim is repetitions rather than measurement, and we will be observing rather than grading closely.

By the end of it you will have taken two passages through the core of an OBT workflow. That is the thing this course is actually for.

items.title: Celebration
items.body: A meal together, a structured debrief on what the week taught each of us, and an introduction to the Psalms workshop that starts on Monday the 24th.

items.title: Thank you for the week you are about to give this.
items.body: Five days is not long to learn a process this size, and the reason it works at all is that everyone in the room does the work rather than watches it. May what we make here serve the communities waiting to hear these passages in their own voice.

blocks.title: Questions during the week
blocks.body: Josh is the first point of contact for anything to do with the course itself.

blocks.title: General travel advice

blocks.title: The ordinary checks, in one place
blocks.body:
Most people coming to an OBT-CDT workshop have travelled internationally many times and do not need to be told any of this. It lives here rather than in a workshop handbook for the few occasions when a reminder is useful: a first long-haul trip, an unfamiliar route, or a participant helping someone else prepare.

Anything specific to a particular workshop, including dates, visas and airport transfers, is on that workshop's own page and takes precedence over what is here.

items.label: Check that the name on your ticket matches your passport exactly.
Keep passport, visa or entry approval, return ticket, insurance and accommodation details together and easy to reach.
Save offline copies of key documents and workshop contacts, and carry one on paper.
Tell the organisers promptly about itinerary changes, accessibility needs, allergies or medical needs.
Check baggage limits for every airline in your itinerary, including domestic and regional legs.
Carry essential medicines in their original packaging, with a prescription or doctor's letter where that helps.
Tell your bank you are travelling, and take more than one way to pay.

blocks.title: Before you leave a workshop base

items.label: Confirm your departure transfer and meeting time. Do not rely on an earlier draft schedule.
Settle personal expenses and follow the base's check-out instructions for your room.
Return keys, access cards, borrowed equipment and workshop materials.
Check drawers, charging points and the bathroom, and label all your luggage.
Leave generous time for the airport and keep your passport where you can reach it.

workshops.title: Narrative
workshops.metaDescription: The first OBT-CDT workshop laid the foundations: OBT-specific exegesis, internalization, oral drafting, and introductory consulting awareness, practiced on biblical narrative.

blocks.title: Narrative
blocks.body: Two weeks in Bangalore, working on story. The first workshop had to establish what OBT exegesis and internalization actually look like before any later genre could build on them.

blocks.title: Why narrative came first
blocks.body:
Narrative came first for a reason: story is the Bible's most accessible genre and the natural on-ramp into oral translation work. The workshop built the foundational OBT skill set: exegesis with an oral lens, internalization of passages through embodied group activities, oral drafting and revision, and a first taste of what consultants listen for in a checking session.

Participants worked in teams through the full OBT cycle on narrative passages, with attention to the things that make or break an oral story: participant reference, story flow, and the storytelling conventions of oral cultures.

blocks.title: Who came
blocks.body:
Around twenty participants gathered in Bangalore from partner organizations across the region: field translators, exegetes, and translation advisors, many already serving active OBT projects. A three-person facilitation team led the two weeks, joined by consultants who provided checking feedback on the teams' work.

For most participants, this workshop was their first step onto the track, and the cohort that formed in Bangalore has continued together through everything since.

blocks.title: What it started
blocks.body: Bangalore established the pattern every later workshop follows: teach only what cannot be gained from books, practice everything, and evaluate through observation rather than examination. It also confirmed the appetite: the interest that surfaced around this first workshop exceeded what one event could hold, and it shaped the plans for everything that followed.

workshops.title: Epistles
workshops.metaDescription: The second OBT-CDT workshop tackled the Epistles: argument structure, discourse prominence, and the series' first mentored consultant checks on a real OBT translation.

blocks.title: Epistles
blocks.body: Two weeks in Chiang Mai on argument rather than story, and the first time participants ran mentored consultant checks on a live oral translation.

blocks.title: A letter lives on its argument
blocks.body:
Epistles ask different questions of a translator than narrative does. Where a story lives on flow and participant reference, a letter lives on its argument: how each move builds on the last, where the emphasis falls, and what the writer is doing with every paragraph.

The second workshop equipped participants with genre-specific exegetical tools for the Epistles, centered on argument structure and discourse prominence, and put those tools to work on passages the teams translated and checked during the two weeks.

blocks.title: A consultant check with real stakes
blocks.body:
The milestone of Chiang Mai was consulting practice with real stakes: participants took part in mentored consultant checking of an actual OBT Epistles translation, observed and guided by experienced consultants.

More than twenty consultants and consultants-in-training worked through the two weeks together, and each one left with a written evaluation grounded in what multiple facilitators had observed across the sessions.

blocks.title: What followed
blocks.body:
After Chiang Mai, the track's between-workshop rhythm took shape: evaluation data from the workshop fed into a series of virtual trainings targeting the competencies participants most needed to strengthen before the Psalms workshop.

The workshop evaluations themselves flowed into each participant's competency record, reviewed with their mentors, adding another layer of documented evidence toward certification.

workshops.title: Psalms
workshops.metaDescription: The third OBT-CDT workshop, in Bali, Indonesia: Hebrew poetry exegesis for OBT and facilitating the translation of Psalms into local artistic genres. Fully booked. This page is also the participant handbook.

blocks.title: Psalms in Bali
blocks.body: The third workshop of the OBT Consultant Development Track, and the participant handbook for it: what the weeks hold, where the base is, what to put in your bag, and what to do before you fly.
blocks.note: Last updated 21 August 2026 · the weekend meal sign-up link is now on this page, in section five, and the Friday deadline is waived for the 22 and 23 August weekend only. Where an older email disagrees with this page, the page is right.

items.label: University of the Nations base, Jimbaran, Bali

blocks.title: This workshop is fully booked
blocks.body: Every place for the Psalms workshop has been filled. If you hoped to join, we would still love to hear from you: expressing interest now puts you in view for the remaining workshops in the series and for future rounds of the track.

blocks.title: Psalms in forms communities already sing
blocks.body:
The Psalms are poetry, and poetry refuses to travel as plain prose. This workshop trains consultants to exegete Hebrew poetry with an oral lens (imagery, parallelism, poetic structure, prominence) and to facilitate the translation of Psalms into the artistic genres a community already sings, chants, and performs.

The overarching framework is the Creating Local Arts Together (CLAT) process: discovering a community's own art forms, matching them to the purposes of a psalm, and creating translations that live as local worship.

blocks.caption: A tingklik player in Bali. The workshop's work is psalms carried in genres a community already plays.

blocks.title: Welcome to Workshop 3
blocks.body:
The Psalter has been the church's most sustained song-and-prayer text for as long as there has been a church. Where Christians have received it as living song, in the musical forms their community already trusts with its most serious speech, it has shaped their theology and their emotional life. Where it has arrived as prose on a page, much less has happened.

Workshop 3 is about that gap. Over these weeks you will exegete Psalms 1 and 13 closely, work alongside mother-tongue translators and artists to craft them in local genres, and then check that work the way a consultant checks aesthetic Scripture.

Some details are still being settled. Where that is true of a section, a panel at the end of it says what is outstanding, so you can tell a tracked gap from an oversight. Read this page rather than a copy you saved earlier.
blocks.caption: A church choir mid-song in Suwon, South Korea.

items.label: Workshop thesis
items.title: The Psalms serve communities most fully when they are translated faithfully into artistic forms local people embrace and use, devotionally and congregationally.
What we are asking of each other

items.label: Listen closely to Scripture, to artists, to translators and to one another.
Practise consultant skills in real cross-cultural team settings.
Connect exegesis, internalisation, artistic translation and community use.
Grow through mentor guidance, peer feedback and reflective practice.

items.body: Work through a psalm deeply yourself, recognise the features of Hebrew poetry that matter for translation, and be able to say what those forms did socially and theologically in their own setting.
Ask culturally appropriate questions to find out what a community actually sings, chants and performs, then analyse the function and features of both psalm genres and candidate local ones.
Lead a contextualised version of the CLAT conversations, holding fidelity to the source and excellence in the target genre at the same time.
Prepare questions suited to aesthetic content, then take a checking conversation from spotting an issue through to resolving it.
Show community leaders inductively why a psalm in a local art form is still a faithful translation, and help artists and translators plan for it to be used.

items.title: What you will be able to do
Facilitators and organisers
items.body: The workshop series is organised jointly by the Global Consultant Pool and SIL Orality Services.

items.body: OBT Researcher, CiT, Translator, and Lead Facilitator of SIL's OBT-CDT. First point of contact for anything related to the workshop itself. Write to josh_frost@sil.org.

items.label: Nikki Mustin
items.body: OBT Consultant & Seasoned Psalms Translation Workshop Facilitator. Leads Psalms exegesis and internalisation, and the checking sessions.

items.body: SIL Global Ethnoarts Consultant & Co-Founder of Scriptura: Psalms Layer-by-Layer. Genre theory, the CLAT process, and translating aesthetic language.

blocks.title: Dates and programme
blocks.body:
Most participants are in Bali for two weeks, 24 August to 4 September. If you are also doing the OBT Crash Course you arrive a week earlier and are there for three.

The Crash Course week has its own handbook, linked under the dates below.

items.label: Independence Day
items.body: Land during the afternoon if your schedule allows. The 17th is Indonesia's national Independence Day, so expect celebrations, red and white everywhere, and slower traffic.

items.label: Five full days
items.body: The OBT Crash Course, for participants who need the shared foundations. It runs Tuesday to Saturday rather than Monday to Friday because the 17th is a public holiday.

items.label: Rest and arrivals
items.body: A rest day. Anyone coming only for the Psalms workshop should be on the base by this evening.

items.label: Two weeks
items.body: Instruction in the mornings; translation and consulting practice with the teams in the afternoons.

items.label: Workshop closes
items.body: Book a late-evening flight that day, or leave on the 5th or later.

items.title: The Crash Course week has its own page
items.body: Everything about the first week lives there. This page carries the logistics for all three weeks, so you need both if your trip starts on the 18th.

items.label: OBT Crash Course handbook
items.body: The philosophy behind the course, the five-day timetable with clock times, and what each of the seventeen sessions is for.

items.title: Check your itinerary against these dates before you book or change anything
items.body: Do not plan to leave before the workshop closes at 5:00 PM on Friday 4 September. If your flights are already booked and they conflict with these dates, tell us now rather than later.

items.title: Which psalms
items.body: The workshop works closely with Psalm 1, a wisdom psalm, and Psalm 13, a lament. Hebrew poetic conventions beyond those two get their own session, so what you learn transfers to the rest of the Psalter.

items.title: The daily rhythm
items.body:
Mornings are theory and skill. Afternoons are application with the mother-tongue translation teams and the artists, and they are also where most competencies get observed and evaluated. Expect around seven hours of classroom time a day, with evening homework kept to no more than ninety minutes.

Every day runs to the same shape: breakfast, then morning teaching sessions with a tea break in the middle, then lunch; afternoon practice sessions with a tea break before dinner.

Each morning opens with a short, Psalms-focused devotional, chosen for that day's work rather than as a generic opener.

items.label: Day 1
items.body:
**Morning:** Opening session and structured introductions between the consultant teams and the artist and translator teams. Aesthetic language and ethnopoetics in the Bible; genre in the Psalms and in cultures.

**Afternoon:** Mapping the genre repertoire of the communities present.

items.label: Day 2
items.body:
**Morning:** CLAT overview, with Scripture goals, genre matching and genre feature analysis.

**Afternoon:** The same three applied to Psalm 1.

items.label: Day 3
items.body:
**Morning:** Translating aesthetic language, CLAT step 5, then Psalm 1 exegesis and an internalisation plan.

**Afternoon:** Facilitating internalisation and beginning to craft Psalm 1 as local art.

items.label: Day 4
items.body:
**Morning:** Debrief of the Psalm 1 process, then Psalm 13 exegesis and internalisation.

**Afternoon:** Refine Psalm 1, match a genre for Psalm 13, begin crafting.

items.label: Day 5
items.body:
**Morning:** Hebrew poetic conventions beyond Psalms 1 and 13, and how to use the Scriptura materials.

**Afternoon:** Psalm 1 refinement and group work on Psalm 13.

items.label: Day 1
items.body:
**Morning:** Community checking and consultant checking of artistic translations, moving into application mid-morning.

**Afternoon:** Helping the teams begin community checking of Psalm 1.

items.label: Day 2
items.body:
**Morning:** Preparing consulting questions and a checking plan for Psalm 1, with real planning time built in.

**Afternoon:** The consultant check itself, then revision.

items.label: Day 3
items.body: **Morning and afternoon:** A full day of checking and revising Psalm 13, carrying on Psalm 1 work where it is needed.

items.label: Day 4
items.body: **Still being decided** between two options: Proverbs, or practice at being a Psalms ambassador to community leaders.

items.label: Day 5
items.body:
**Morning:** Integration conversations and APPLY conversations with the artists.

**Afternoon:** Finalising integration plans, each group performing Psalms 1 and 13, and the closing ceremony.

blocks.title: Your preparation
blocks.body: The workshop is most fruitful when people arrive having already done the preparatory work. We consider it foundational: it shapes what you understand when you walk in, and how much help you can be to the translation teams. If you have hit obstacles, tell us. We would much rather talk it through than have you arrive feeling behind.
blocks.caption: The Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete manuscript of the Hebrew Bible and the base text behind the Hebrew you will be reading.

items.title: Exegesis of the two psalms
items.body: Study Psalm 1 first, then Psalm 13, using the Exegetical Guide (linked beneath). Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm; Psalm 13 is a lament. The cohort schedule asked for Psalm 1 by 20 May and Psalm 13 by 8 June.

items.title: If you joined late
items.body: Do not try to recover the original dates. Start now and count from today: roughly two weeks on Psalm 1, then three on Psalm 13, with Hebrew reading practice running alongside in small amounts. If you are joining very close to the workshop, begin with Psalm 1 and ask us to help you prioritise the rest.

items.title: Hebrew reading fluency
items.body: Keep your Hebrew reading moving. Listening while following the Hebrew text is a good way to stay motivated and to get the rhythm of the poetry into your ear. The resources below were Katie's suggestions to the cohort.

items.title: Prepare your posture as well as your notes
items.body:
Pray for humility, attentiveness, creativity and a servant-hearted way of consulting. Come ready to learn from mother-tongue translators, from artists, from peers and from mentors, and expect feedback to change both your thinking and your work.

It also helps to notice, before you arrive, how poetry, song, lament, praise and wisdom already function in your own cultural setting.

items.label: Exegetical Guide
items.body: The guide the exegesis prework follows, for both psalms.

items.label: MiQedem: Psalm 13
items.body: The full text, sung in Hebrew.

items.label: MiQedem: Psalm 1
items.body: The first half of the psalm.

items.label: Mechon Mamre audio
items.body: Read recordings covering all the passages.

items.label: Biblical eLearning: Psalm 1
items.body: Hebrew read aloud with English subtitles.

items.label: Biblical eLearning: Psalm 13
items.body: Hebrew read aloud with English subtitles.

items.label: Prerequisite
items.title: This prework assumes you have already done an OBT Crash Course, or have equivalent experience
items.body: If you have not, the Crash Course from 18 to 22 August is the route in, and it changes how you prepare. Check with Josh so you are pointed the right way.

items.title: Sharing workshop material
items.body: Upload only workshop-relevant material and use filenames someone else can understand. Do not circulate participant information, recordings or community materials beyond the permissions you have been given.

blocks.title: Travel, visas and packing
blocks.body: Book against the dates in section 2, then tell us what you booked. Everything the organisers arrange for you, from visas to the ride from the airport, is planned off the flight details on your registration form.
blocks.caption: The international terminal at I Gusti Ngurah Rai, built in Balinese style.

items.title: When to arrive
items.body:
If you are joining the Crash Course, plan to be in Bali on Monday 17 August, during the afternoon. If you are coming only for the Psalms workshop, be on the base by Sunday 23 August.

You are very welcome to come a couple of days early and stay at the base beforehand. We especially encourage that for anyone crossing four or five time zones or more. A day or two lets your body catch up so you can work properly from the first session instead of pushing through jet lag.

items.title: When to leave
items.body: The workshop ends at 5:00 PM on Friday 4 September. Choose a late-evening flight that day, or leave on the 5th or later. Leave real time for the drive to the airport, check-in, security and immigration.

items.title: Fill in the registration form, and add your flight details as soon as they are booked
items.body:
The form link is in the email we sent you. Write to Josh if you cannot find it. One form covers the whole event, so if you are attending both weeks you fill it in once. We use it to arrange visas, accommodation and airport pickups.

We need your airline, flight number, arrival and departure dates and times, and a mobile or WhatsApp number we can reach you on.

If you are travelling on a passport that does not get visa on arrival and you will need an invitation letter, say so on the form as early as you can. Those take time to arrange.

items.title: Airport transfers
items.body:
We have budgeted to cover your transport between the airport and the base, and we arrange it from the flight details on the registration form. Getting yours in early is what lets us group arrivals so nobody waits long after landing.

The vans are planned around the arrival times we already hold. If we do not have yours, we cannot promise to cover your ride, and you may have to arrange and pay for it yourself. We would far rather meet you at the airport, so send what you know even if the flight is not booked yet.

Wait for a direct confirmation before you assume your pickup is booked. If your flight changes, tell us: we re-plan pickups around actual landing times, but only if we know.

items.label: General travel advice
items.body: The ordinary pre-flight and departure checks, kept off this page. Skim it if you want the reminder; most of you will not need it.

items.label: Check before you travel
items.title: Entry rules depend on your nationality and they change
items.body: Every participant is responsible for checking official Indonesian immigration guidance for the passport they will actually travel on.

items.label: Passport
items.body: Official guidance commonly asks for at least six months' validity.

items.label: Visa
items.body: Apply for the ordinary 30-day tourist visa, the B1 Visa on Arrival, through the official portal below. Do not select "work and travel": that is a separate category and it requires a sponsor inside Indonesia. Some passports, ASEAN ones among them, enter visa-free for 30 days, and that works just as well.

items.label: Arrival declaration
items.body: The immigration portal requires an arrival card, submitted within the three days before you arrive. Submitting it returns a QR code. Keep it on your phone: you show it at the checkpoint after immigration.

items.label: Onward travel
items.body: Carry evidence of a return or onward ticket in case it is asked for.

items.label: Bali levy
items.body: International tourists generally pay the Bali Tourism Levy of IDR 150,000 per person. Keep the voucher.
Use government portals only. Do not use agents, or links forwarded to you without checking where they go.

items.title: What to bring
items.body:
For the workshop itself: a laptop and charger, a notebook, and headphones good enough for careful listening to audio. Facilitators may ask for specific Psalms materials or recording gear closer to the date.

Beyond that, pack for the tropics. Late August and early September fall in Bali's dry season, and they are the two driest months of its year: daytime highs of about 29 to 30°C (84 to 86°F), nights around 25°C (77°F), humid throughout, and roughly 40 to 50 mm of rain across a whole month, falling on three or four days as a short heavy shower rather than a wet day. Bring light, breathable clothing, one layer for strong air-conditioning, something modest for worship and for visits to religious or cultural sites, and shoes you can stand in all day. Bring a light blanket for your bed as well; the base does not provide one, and there is more on that under Rooming.

Bali also has some of the most beautiful beaches in the world and you should enjoy them. Bring whatever you need to do that safely in equatorial sun: swimwear, a hat, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen.

items.label: Complete the workshop evaluation and any consultant-development follow-up.
Save the final shared resources, and note the permissions attached before you use community materials.
Stay in touch with mentors and peers through whatever channels the group agrees on.

blocks.title: Life on the base
blocks.body: Jimbaran sits just south of the airport on Bali's Bukit peninsula.

items.value: University of the Nations base, Jimbaran

items.value: Yayasan Putra Pemenang, Tiara Nusa, Jl. Goa Gong, Jimbaran, Bali, Indonesia

Open the address in Google Maps

items.title: Our hosts
items.body: We are guests here. Part of the reason this workshop can happen at a cost that lets fifty people attend is the real generosity of the base, and that shapes some of the practical arrangements further down, meals in particular.

items.title: Rooming
items.body:
You are welcome to stay at the base for the workshop, and accommodation has been planned for confirmed participants. We are working from the base's own rooming layout, and where we can we are pairing people who share a language.

**Bring your own blanket.** The base sheets every bed and gives you a pillow with a case, but it does not provide blankets. The rooms are air-conditioned and nights outside sit around 25°C, so this is about sleeping comfortably rather than keeping warm. If you are travelling a long way and would rather not carry one, write to Josh as soon as you can and we will buy one here for about $4.

items.title: The teaching space
items.body: The base is setting up the main teaching room with a projector and screen, a whiteboard, and a sound system with microphones, which matters for the music work. Reliable internet in that room is part of the request.

items.title: Meals and dietary needs
items.body:
Meals come through the base kitchen on working days. Part of what keeps the cost low enough for fifty people to attend is the generosity of our hosts, and one of the ways the base runs efficiently is by having large visiting groups help with meal preparation and cleanup.

We will organise that so those who are able-bodied share the work and it finishes quickly together, rather than anyone losing half an afternoon session to it.

items.title: Weekends
items.body:
The base kitchen does not serve as many meals at the weekend, so we give you a small stipend and you buy your own nearby: roughly Rp 50,000 for the whole weekend, about $3. That is not meant to cover every weekend meal on its own. The two arrangements below are what make it enough. When you do eat out, choose places that follow normal food-safety practice.

We eat together twice each weekend, on Saturday evening and again on Sunday evening. The meal is cooked on the base and costs you nothing. **You need to opt in by the Friday before.** The kitchen shops on Friday for the whole weekend, so a name added on Saturday cannot be fed. Signing up is a short form that takes a few seconds, and you can submit it again if your plans change. The link is on the card below.

**For the first weekend, 22 and 23 August, that Friday deadline does not apply.** The link reached you later than it should have, which is our doing rather than yours, so the kitchen will cook from whatever we have by Saturday morning. The Friday rule starts with the weekend of 29 and 30 August.

Each weekend you also get three packets of instant noodles and three eggs as a supplement. They are yours to eat whenever you like: a late arrival, a skipped breakfast, or supper in your room.

items.label: Sign up for the weekend meals
items.note: Sign up by the Friday before each weekend. You can submit it again if your plans change.

items.title: Tell us about allergies and medically necessary dietary requirements, in writing
items.body: If you have not already done so, put it on the registration form or email it. An informal conversation is not something the kitchen can work from.

items.title: Staying online

items.label: Download the documents you need before you travel, and keep an offline copy.
Do not count on workshop Wi-Fi for large uploads or continuous video calls.
A local SIM or eSIM is worth considering if you need reliable data of your own.
Take normal care on shared networks, and do not post the Wi-Fi password anywhere public.

items.body: Plan for less bandwidth than you have at home.

items.title: Laundry
items.body:
For most participants the workshop runs two weeks, and for anyone also doing the Crash Course it runs three. Pack with laundry in mind either way.

The base recommends a laundry near us that collects and delivers. Students on the base have used it and been looked after well. Message them on WhatsApp to arrange a pickup; they work by the kilogram, and you choose how fast you need it back.

items.title: What the laundry charges
items.body: Read off their own price list in August 2026, converted at roughly Rp 17,800 to the US dollar. Prices and turnaround are theirs to change, so confirm both, and what each service covers, when you message them.

items.label: Wash and fold
items.body: About $0.35, back in two days. Rp 10,000 for next day, about $0.55. Rp 14,000 for three hours, about $0.80.

items.label: Cuci komplit
items.body: Full service. About $0.45, back in two days. Rp 12,000 for next day, about $0.70. Rp 16,000 for three hours, about $0.90.

items.label: Strika or kering
items.body: Ironing or drying only. About $0.35, back in two days. Rp 9,000 for next day, about $0.50. Rp 12,000 for three hours, about $0.70.

items.title: Free time and exploring together
items.body:
Bali has a great deal to offer and you are warmly welcome to enjoy it. To be clear, the facilitators are not organising or sponsoring outings.

In past workshops participants decided together where they wanted to go, pooled money for a van, and went as a group. Some very good memories came out of that. We would love it to happen again, organised among yourselves.

items.label: Indonesia emergency
items.body: The national emergency line, reachable from any phone.

items.label: Workshop contact
items.body: Josh Frost, lead facilitator.

blocks.title: Cost and financial support
blocks.body: Room and board in Bali is covered, as participants were told in March. Nobody is being asked to pay to attend. The figures below are a recommended contribution, and they are a guide rather than a bill.

items.label: OBT Crash Course
items.body: Five days, 18 to 22 August.

items.label: Psalms workshop
items.body: Two weeks, 24 August to 4 September.

items.label: Both weeks
items.body: For someone here from the Crash Course through to the close.

items.title: If your organisation has a training budget
items.body: Where your organisation has a line for professional development, a contribution toward the workshop is welcome and it does real work. Contributions from participants whose organisations have funding are what let grant money reach participants whose organisations have nothing at all for training. If yours would like to give, write to Josh and he will arrange the invoice.

items.title: From the workshop after Bali onward
items.body:
Grants and donations have carried the whole cost of this track so far, and that is not a foundation a two-and-a-half-year programme can be built on. So each workshop after Bali will carry a participation cost.

That cost is built from room and board for the stay, the flights for the facilitators who travel in to teach, and the materials a workshop runs on, down to the paper participants draft, colour and mark up on while they internalise a passage. It will be set a little above what those come to, and the difference is deliberate: it funds scholarships for participants whose organisations cannot send them. Each figure will differ from venue to venue and will be named once that venue is settled.

items.title: If cost would ever keep you from a workshop
items.body: Partial and full scholarships are available, and no qualified participant is kept from a workshop over money. Write to Josh Frost directly. You will not be asked to document or justify your situation in detail, and the conversation stays between the two of you.

items.title: May this shared work strengthen the translation of the Psalms into forms communities will actually sing.

blocks.title: If you missed this one
blocks.body: Two workshops remain in the series, and expressions of interest now shape their planning.
